source.excerpt: Then perhaps he can be what he is, openly and without fear.
trail: Wikiquote identifies page 66 of On Becoming a Person and explicitly introduces the circulating sentence as a paraphrase.

The genuine passage discusses a therapist being transparent about his own experience so that the other person can be open without fear. The short excerpt here is its concluding sentence, not the popular paraphrase.
The inspected AGRIS/National Agricultural Library record confirms the 1961 book and its clinical and interpersonal subject matter. The original page was not inspected.

author.bio: Carl Rogers (1902–1987) was an American psychologist associated with humanistic psychology and person-centered psychotherapy. His work studied the helping relationship and conditions for personal growth; On Becoming a Person gathers reflections on therapy, learning and interpersonal relationships.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Rogers’s original passage concerns openness within therapy, including the therapist’s willingness to be transparent in a relationship. The familiar shortened version turns that relational discussion into a personal affirmation. Keeping the distinction preserves both his authorship and the more specific setting of his argument.

schema.faqAnswer: The sentence paraphrases Carl Rogers’s longer passage in On Becoming a Person (1961), p. 66. His original discusses a therapist’s transparency and the other person’s ability to be open without fear; it is not this exact short affirmation.
schema.verdictNote: The documented Quotation is a short concluding sentence from the source passage. The popular display wording is a paraphrase, not an authenticated verbatim sentence.
